description: We are Team Aquila from Rajshahi, Bangladesh: MD. Abu Bokkor (developer and researcher) and Mst. Maharun Nasha Queen (designer). Every fire season, crews ask one question: is this season normal? NASA satellites hold the answer, but the record is split between MODIS and VIIRS. Our project FireLens harmonizes 26 years of NASA FIRMS hotspots into one burning activity calendar, giving responders worldwide early warning. The sensor no longer matters. The fire does.
summary: FireLens is a web app that turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning activity calendar for any place on Earth. The fire record is split between two sensors: MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012), which sees about four times more fire, so global detections jump from 4.3 to 17.5 million in 2012 even though fire did not. FireLens harmonizes them with a gradient-boosted model trained on the years both satellites flew together, converting VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent counts and producing one record of about half a billion detections from 2000 to today (R² 0.94 on years it never saw, in 211 countries). Users pick any area and dates to see which months and years burn most, how this month compares with its 2003–2025 median, unusual weeks with an eight-week outlook, live fires and email alerts, and download every result as CSV and charts. Emergency responders get early warning, scientists a trustworthy long-term record, and land managers a plan for the critical fire season. The sensor no longer matters. The fire does.
details:
FireLens is a full-stack web application that harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records into one burning activity calendar, so the sensor of origin no longer matters and patterns, trends and anomalies become the focus.

How it works:

Every NASA FIRMS detection since November 2000 (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS Suomi NPP and NOAA-20) is cleaned to vegetation fires and gridded into 0.25° cells by week. A gradient-boosted Poisson model learns how both sensors see the same fire, from VIIRS count, fire radiative power, night share, latitude, season and each cell's long-run ratio, then converts VIIRS into MODIS-equivalent detections. A local factor anchors every area to its own MODIS record, NASA's missing-data table corrects satellite outages, and NOAA-20 fills Suomi NPP gaps. The archive (647 monthly NASA files) lives on Cloudflare R2 and is updated every day from the FIRMS near-real-time feed.

Key features:

- Any area: search, click a country, draw a box, upload GeoJSON, or enter latitude and longitude.

- Any dates, down to one day, with the same dates in every year since 2000 ranked against the 2003–2025 median.

- A monthly or weekly calendar since 2000 with the critical period and colour-blind-safe ramps.

- Unusual conditions and an eight-week outlook; live fires, hourly email alerts and a printable area report.

- Downloads: every hotspot as CSV, tables, PNG charts, map, or one ZIP.

Benefits and intended impact:

Responders see a season turning before it peaks, scientists get one consistent 26-year record, and land managers can plan patrols and burn bans around the critical period — free, open source, for every country.

Does it work:

Tested on 2022–2026 in 211 countries, the model reaches R² 0.941 against 0.909 for a single global ratio (India 0.94 vs 0.63, Canada 0.93 vs 0.67). Without being told, it finds Canada 2023 as the highest of 27 years and, for the challenge's own Chilecito, Argentina fire, shows 25 July–25 August 2026 at 2.9× the median.

Burning activity calendar for Canada: 2023 stands out as the highest of 27 years.

Tools and technologies:

Python (pandas, PyArrow, DuckDB, scikit-learn, Shapely), FastAPI on Google Cloud Run, React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS and Tailwind CSS on Cloudflare Pages, Cloudflare R2 storage, Firestore and Resend for alerts.

Creativity:

Instead of one global conversion factor, FireLens learns how the sensors differ by place and season and keeps the record alive as satellites retire — then turns 26 years of data into a calendar a fire officer can read in seconds.

Design considerations:

Scientific honesty (two-week statistics as the MODIS user guide advises, provisional near-real-time weeks marked, limits stated), accessibility (no login, plain labels, colour-blind-safe colours, works on phones), low running cost, and full reproducibility.
